title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, as quoted by Warren Buffett in the 2008 Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter

web_blocks.html: Chapters 1 to 6 judged the business without looking at a quote. This chapter puts a price on it. The verified ledger close is ₹2,297.00 (NSE, 12 November 2026), and all valuation figures here are struck at that price. A later TradingView pull, taken after the 13 November close, shows ₹2,259.30 (−1.64% on the day). It is not yet ledger-verified, so I call it the 13 Nov print and use it only where it changes an answer. The two prices are never blended. The share count is 17,105,816 (1.7106 Cr) and has not changed since the FY22 buyback [1]. Market capitalisation is therefore ₹3,929.2 Cr at the ledger close and ₹3,865 Cr at the print. Management-defined cash was ₹163 Cr at 30 September 2026. There is no bank debt, because the Unbound term loan was repaid in August [2]. Add about ₹18 Cr of lease liabilities and enterprise value is roughly ₹3,784 Cr.

web_blocks.takeaway: At ₹2,297.00 the stock costs about 21 times trailing earnings, 18 times our FY27 estimate and 12 times forward EBITDA. The free-cash-flow yield is 5-6% and the return on capital is 35-39%. That is the profile of a good business at a fair price. It is not a distressed bargain and it is not a bubble. The table cannot show one thing. The FY27 EBITDA estimate is already about 33% above FY26, so recent growth is in the ratios. What remains to be earned is the next leg, FY28.

web_blocks.html: The first honest conclusion is modest. MPS is not cheap enough to buy on valuation alone. It is not so expensive that valuation is the reason to stay away. Everything depends on whether the earnings base can keep rising while an AI-deflation debate presses on the multiple. The next sections test that in three steps: where the multiple has been, what the price already assumes, and how peers are priced.

web_blocks.caption: MPS price-to-earnings band, weekly, June 2016 to 12 November 2026 (trailing financial-year EPS applied from 1 June)
rows: The multiple of an ex-growth, acquisition-digesting company
Equals the five-year median; near the 75th percentile of the ten-year band
Our bull-case multiple is 22x, just below
Last five years: min / median / max
Today is dead centre of the recent band
web_blocks.takeaway: Today's 22.7x on FY26 EPS is exactly the five-year median. It sits near the 75th percentile of the full ten-year band. The multiple is therefore not depressed against recent history, and it is above the ten-year median of 17.6x. The stock is mid-pack against the last five years and rich-ish against the decade. It is a bargain on neither. The desk computed the band from the ledger price history and the aggregator's financial-year EPS. Each year's EPS is applied from 1 June after the fiscal year-end.

web_blocks.caption: Cycle endpoints on the same trailing-EPS basis: price, multiple and what drove it
rows: Cash-rich, slow-growing content-services business at a 36% EBITDA margin [76]
Down 57.7% in 46 months; EBITDA margin had slid to 26% on acquired businesses
Up 1,416% in 59 months; FY25 EPS was about to rise 25.4% to ₹87.05
Down 51.9% in 11 months while FY26 EPS rose 16.3% to ₹101.26
Up 110.5% in five months on a first-half EBITDA rise of 39% [2]
21.6% below the August close high; ledger Stage 3, snapshot Stage 4
web_blocks.takeaway: Three drawdowns of 50% or more since 2015 (−57.7%, −67.5%, −51.9%) are the base rate for this stock. The latest one happened while earnings grew. Between March 2025 and March 2026, trailing EPS rose from ₹69.43 to ₹87.05. Yet the multiple fell from 41.7x to 16.0x, a 61.6% compression. That accounts for more than the whole price fall. The multiple, not the earnings, is the volatile variable in this stock.

web_blocks.html: Why was 41.7x so high in March 2025? The market was capitalising an earnings-acceleration phase. EPS grew from ₹63.83 in FY23 to ₹69.43 in FY24 (+8.8%). It then jumped to ₹87.05 in FY25 (+25.4%) and ₹101.26 in FY26 (+16.3%) [76]. FY25 revenue grew 33%, and most of that came from the AJE acquisition. FY26 revenue growth was back to 6% [1]. A multiple measured on FY24 EPS looked absurd at 41.7x. Forward earnings were about to catch up, so the buyer was paying for FY25, not FY24. The 2023-25 multiple was inflated by that acceleration. It was also inflated by a market that extrapolated acquisition-fuelled growth. Once EPS growth settles in the mid-teens, a multiple between 17x and 23x is the sensible neighbourhood. That range runs from the ten-year median to the five-year median.

Why did the multiple then fall to 16.0x by March 2026? That multiple sat near the ten-year 25th percentile of 13.8x and above the November 2019 level of 14.4x. The honest answer is that it was not about MPS alone. In February and March 2026 an AI-disintermediation debate swept almost every labour-based services and information name. The dated record follows. Two of the sources are broker and aggregator blogs whose figures wobble between headline and body. I use them for date and order of magnitude, not for decimals.

web_blocks.takeaway: MPS touched its 2026 low in the very week the Indian IT index made its own. The de-rating from 41.7x to 16.0x was a sector repricing, not a company-specific discovery. That is the good news. The uncomfortable half is the next line. The peers have not recovered, and MPS did. Its one-year change of roughly −0.6% is a round trip (−51.9%, then +110.5%) rather than a stable plateau.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: a multiple is a mood about the terminal value
paragraphs: When earnings rise 25% and the multiple falls 60%, the market is not disagreeing about next year. It is changing its mind about the years after that. The 2026 AI debate is a debate about terminal value. Will content-production vendors still keep a margin in 2032? Nobody can answer that with a forecast, which is why the multiple swings so far.

The disciplined response is neither to buy the fear nor to wait for certainty. Work out what the price assumes about the years after next. Then ask whether our evidence is better or worse than that assumption. The reverse DCF that follows does exactly that.

web_blocks.html: Now the reverse DCF. Instead of forecasting and asking what the stock is worth, I take the price. I hold the discount rate and terminal growth fixed. Then I solve for the free-cash-flow growth that the price requires. The starting point is FY27E free cash flow to the firm of ₹214 Cr. It is built from EBITDA of ₹315 Cr, less 25% tax on EBIT after ₹36 Cr of depreciation, less ₹11 Cr of capex, ₹5 Cr of lease payments and a ₹15 Cr working-capital build. That is a 5.7% yield on EV. Growth then fades in a straight line over ten years, from the solved year-one rate to the terminal rate. I chose a fade because no business sustains 15% growth and then drops to 5% in year eleven. The model is the desk's own, in valuation.py. The grid extends it around the four central cases.

web_blocks.the_number: At ₹2,297.00 the market pays for free cash flow that starts at ₹214 Cr in FY27. If you demand a 13% return, the average annual growth along the fade path is 8.8% over ten years, with 12.6% in year one fading to 5%. The constant-rate equivalent is 9.2% a year.
web_blocks.how_calculated: This is a reverse discounted cash flow. Enterprise value of ₹3,784 Cr is set equal to ten years of free cash flow to the firm plus a terminal value. We solve for the year-one growth rate. Growth fades in a straight line to the terminal rate by year ten.
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY27E free cash flow to the firm of ₹214 Cr. It uses EBITDA ₹315 Cr, D&A ₹36 Cr, tax 25% on EBIT, capex ₹11 Cr, leases ₹5 Cr and a working-capital build of ₹15 Cr. The discount rate is 13% and terminal growth is 5%. Free cash flow reaches about ₹496 Cr by year ten.
web_blocks.the_range: At 12% and 5% terminal growth the price needs 9.1% in year one (about 7.0% a year on average). At 14% and 5% it needs 15.9% (about 10.4%). At 13% and 4% it needs 15.0% (about 9.5%). Across the full 11-15% by 3-6% grid the answer runs from 1.7% to 22.9%. The discount rate matters more than any other single assumption.
web_blocks.if_off: If your hurdle is 14% rather than 13%, the price needs about 3 more points of year-one growth. That is hard against the FY15-26 EBITDA CAGR of 10.2%. It is easy against the FY21-26 CAGR of 17.1%. If free cash flow grows only 8% a year for ten years, a buyer at ₹2,297 earns about 12.4% a year.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF grid: implied year-one growth in free cash flow (%), fading linearly to terminal growth over ten years, at EV ₹3,784 Cr and FY27E FCFF ₹214 Cr
web_blocks.takeaway: Read the 12-14% rows and the 4-5% columns. They bracket a sensible Indian small-cap hurdle and the long-run growth of a USD-earning business. The market needs year-one growth of roughly 9% to 18% in that zone. The 13% and 5% cell (12.6%) is the central case. The harsh corner is 3% terminal growth with a 15% hurdle (22.9%). That is where the AI bears effectively live. They assume the franchise has little growth after year ten and demand a high return for the risk.

web_blocks.caption: What a buyer at ₹2,297.00 earns if free cash flow grows at a constant rate for ten years, then 5% (EV ₹3,784 Cr; start ₹214 Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: If MPS merely repeats its longest-run EBITDA growth of 10.2%, the buyer earns about 13.5% a year. If it repeats the last five years (17.1%), the return is about 17.7%. A constant 9.2% for ten years is what a 13% return needs. It is 7.2% at a 12% return and 11.1% at 14%. The price therefore assumes a decent decade. That is below what the company delivered in the last five years and roughly equal to what it delivered over eleven.

web_blocks.html: Now put that against delivered history and guidance. EBITDA compounded at 17.1% from FY21 to FY26 and at 10.2% from FY15 to FY26. Sales compounded at 12.7% and 11.9% over the same windows [76]. Both EBITDA windows include acquisitions, and AJE in FY25 was the main one. The FY21 base was also depressed by the pandemic and a 37% tax rate, so the 17.1% flatters. The FY27 guide is a floor of ₹310 Cr, raised from ₹300 Cr on 4 November. H1 FY27 EBITDA was ₹154 Cr. The CFO said: “We are now raising the floor, and we expect FY27 EBITDA to be at least INR310 crores.” (CFO Prarthana Agarwal, Q2 FY27) [2] That is +31% on FY26's ₹236 Cr, and our desk figure of ₹315 Cr is +33%. Our FY27E free cash flow already contains it. The Vision-2027 destination is ₹450 Cr of EBITDA and ₹1,500 Cr of revenue in FY28. The CEO told the Q1 FY27 call that this “probably will translate to more like INR450 crores EBITDA.” (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q1 FY27) [25] That is 43% above our FY27E. The CEO himself says the revenue target combines organic growth with acquisitions. Our base case of ₹360 Cr is 14% above FY27E and needs no deal.

Read together, the price assumes something close to the middle of delivered history, not the top. It does not pay for Vision-2027. At ₹360 Cr of base FY28E EBITDA the forward P/E is 16.0x on FY28E EPS of ₹143.4. That is a forward multiple, so it is not comparable with the trailing band. On base LTM EPS at the value date (₹133.9) the multiple is 17.2x. On FY27E EPS of ₹124.5, which is the band's own basis, it is 18.4x. A figure of ₹450 Cr would be a large upside surprise. That is the case for the stock. The case against is where the market's scepticism sits. It explains why a business this good is not priced higher. (1) AI price give-back. The CEO's own words are that “Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume” (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q2 FY27) [2]. A 20% unit-price cut needs 25% more volume to hold revenue. The evidence that MPS keeps the savings is essentially one segment's margin trend. (2) Research margin durability. Research is about 60% of revenue and about 65% of segment EBITDA. Its margin climbed from roughly 37-42% a year ago to 48.2% in Q2 FY27 [2]. On FY26 Research revenue of ₹463.5 Cr, every point of margin is about ₹4.6 Cr of EBITDA. A return to 40% would remove about ₹37 Cr, which is the arithmetic of our bear case [1]. (3) Concentration. The largest customer was 17.3% of FY26 revenue and the top 15 were 58% [1]. (4) Acquisition accounting. Goodwill plus acquired intangibles are 52.5% of total assets. The Unbound purchase-price allocation is provisional until February 2027. Corporate Learning carries ₹100.4 Cr of goodwill against a segment result of ₹11.3 Cr [1]. None of the four is a flaw in the audited record. Each is a reason the market refuses to pay 29x again.

Now the peers. Three listed Indian companies share enough DNA with MPS to deserve a table. Datamatics sells publishing and data services through Lumina Datamatics and TNQTech. NIIT Learning Systems runs managed training services. Newgen Software builds content and process platforms. None is a clean comparable. All three are in Stage 4 under the snapshot classifier. The table is rendered from the 13 November TradingView pull.

web_blocks.caption: MPS and listed Indian peers: valuation, profitability, leverage and one-year move (13 November 2026 snapshot)
web_blocks.takeaway: MPS has the highest margin in the set, at a 29.45% TTM operating margin against 12.9% to 23.7%. It also has the highest ROCE and the least leverage. Its P/E of 20.74 is the highest in the set, against Datamatics at 18.87, Newgen at 19.6 and NIIT Learning Systems at 9.87. MPS trades about 10% above Datamatics and about 6% above Newgen. In return it gets almost twice the operating margin and almost twice the ROCE of Datamatics (38.7% against 20.4%). The one-year column is the real signal. The three peers are down 18-56% while MPS is roughly flat. The AI de-rating is still open for them. For MPS it is largely done, and then reversed. That is a reason to respect the market's verdict, and a warning that MPS has already had its relief rally. TradingView's ₹3,934 Cr market cap for MPS uses a different share count from our ₹3,865 Cr (₹2,259.30 × 1.7106 Cr shares). It is shown for peer comparison only.

web_blocks.caption: Global comparables: what verified numbers say about the AI and price-deflation debate (no prices quoted)
rows: Language and content services; the live test of price deflation from machine translation
Adjusted PBT £60.4m against £106.7m, about 8.8% against 14.9% of revenue (desk arithmetic); £88.0m goodwill impairment
Per-unit price deflation is not theoretical. It cut a services margin by about 6 points in one year, which is why the 'AI price give-back' bear case is credible. MPS has so far gone the other way.
Clinical decision support (UpToDate) and nursing content
Proprietary, expert-authored content plus AI raises margin rather than lowering it. This is the template for Unbound's ambition; Unbound is about $9m of revenue [25].
Data engineering and human expertise for AI builders
Q3 2026 revenue $95.6m, +53%; FY26 growth guide 42% or more [88]
Adjusted gross margin 40%; adjusted EBITDA 18.5% of revenue

AI creates demand for human judgment, but at at-will, project-based contracts, lumpy customers and an 18.5% margin. Growth is not the same as quality: MPS's 30%+ EBITDA margin and recurring base are a higher-quality, slower stream.
The corporate-learning profit pool is shrinking for scale players too. This is why we treat Corporate Learning (13% of MPS revenue) as a watch item, not an engine.
Lumina Datamatics and TNQTech, subsidiaries of Datamatics Global Services
Group FY26 revenue ₹1,987.2 Cr, +15.3% (publishing arm not disclosed separately) [62]
Group EBITDA ₹371.6 Cr, 18.7% of revenue (desk arithmetic), against MPS's 30.7% in FY26

The direct Indian competitor grows faster at a 12-point lower margin. Either MPS's platform, journal and author-services mix earns the gap or it is the first thing a price-aggressive rival attacks. This is the margin the bears target.
web_blocks.takeaway: Two firms in the table show deflation or shrinkage. They are RWS and Skillsoft. Two show that AI-era demand rewards proprietary content or scarce human judgment. They are Wolters Kluwer Health and Innodata. The Indian peer shows the margin gap. MPS spans all of these, so it is neither a clean AI winner nor a clean loser. It owns journals, platforms and a medical-knowledge asset that behave like Wolters Kluwer's. It also has a large production book that behaves like RWS's. The valuation question is how the profit pool is split between the two over the next five years.

web_blocks.html: Now to the scenarios. We value the stock twelve months ahead, around November 2027. A trailing multiple must be applied to trailing earnings, so the valuation shows two readings. The ten-year band is built on last-reported fiscal-year EPS. At a November 2027 value date, that basis means FY27E EPS. We call it basis A, and it is the stress case. Markets price on current earnings while the band lags, so we also show basis B. It uses last-twelve-months (LTM) EPS at the value date, the average of FY27E and FY28E EPS. Basis B is the more generous reading and our central case. The first table uses basis B. The two-basis table after it shows both. All cases assume D&A of ₹36 Cr in FY27E and ₹38 Cr in FY28E, other income of ₹8 Cr, interest of ₹3 Cr, a 25% tax rate and 1.7106 Cr shares. Only EBITDA and the multiple change. The multiples are anchored on the band measured above, not invented. Bear 14x is near the 25th percentile (13.8x). Base 18x is near the ten-year median (17.6x). Bull 22x is near the five-year median (22.7x). The bull case needs no multiple expansion beyond where the stock trades today.

web_blocks.caption: Basis B (central case): probability-weighted 12-month valuation on LTM EPS at the value date (about November 2027)
web_blocks.takeaway: On basis B the probability-weighted value of ₹2,440 is only 6.2% above the ledger close. On valuation alone the stock is close to fairly priced. The spread runs from −29.1% to +44.1%. The upside-to-downside ratio of the extreme cases is 1.5 to 1, and the base case offers just +4.9%. A 29% loss is what we would live with if the AI-deflation argument is right. This is an adequate business at an adequate price. It is not a margin of safety. The picture improves with a lower entry. The same weights give +13.5% from ₹2,150 and +17.9% from ₹2,070. The base value of ₹2,410 is 19.4x FY27E EPS of ₹124.5, between the ten-year median and the 75th percentile.

web_blocks.caption: Two earnings bases for the same scenarios: A (year-end EPS, the band's own basis) and B (LTM EPS at the value date)
rows: B. LTM EPS at the value date (116.4 / 133.9 / 150.4), same multiples
web_blocks.takeaway: Basis A is the band's own basis, so it is the stricter test. On basis A the base value is ₹2,241, which is 2.4% below the ledger close. The weighted value is ₹2,254, which is 1.9% below it. Basis B gives ₹2,440. We treat B as central because markets price on current earnings, while the band is built on a lagging EPS. Basis A therefore understates what the market typically pays. We keep it as the stress case and size the position so the verdict survives it. The 25/50/25 weights are also a judgment. Moving to 35/45/20 would lower the basis B weighted value to about ₹2,317. The verdict does not depend on the weights. The decision rule is reward-to-risk at the support zone.

web_blocks.caption: Reward-to-risk on the base value by entry price (invalidation: daily close below ₹2,005; hurdle 1.5 to 1)
rows: No on either basis; on A the base is below the price
web_blocks.takeaway: The ₹2,070 level clears the hurdle on both bases, so it is the core entry. The ₹2,150 level clears it only on basis B. It needs a base value of at least ₹2,367.50. Basis B clears that line by 1.8%. Basis A misses it by ₹126.5. On basis A the line needs FY27E EPS of about ₹131.5, which is FY27 EBITDA of roughly ₹331 Cr. That is why the top of the zone is conditional and the bottom is not.

web_blocks.caption: What has to happen in each scenario, and why that multiple
rows: AI price give-back, a Corporate Learning stall and an acquisition stumble. Research margin falls back to about 40%. FY27 lands on ₹300 Cr, just under the ₹310 Cr floor. FY28E EBITDA is ₹295 Cr, 6% below the base FY27E.
14x is near the 25th percentile (13.8x). It is the multiple of a company whose growth has stopped.
FY27 guide of at least ₹310 Cr delivered, at ₹315 Cr. FY28 EBITDA grows about 14% to ₹360 Cr at a margin of about 33-34%. No acquisition is needed.
18x is near the ten-year median (17.6x). It is a normal multiple for normal compounding.
Acquisitions plus Research margin near 50% and an Education recovery. FY27 EBITDA is ₹330 Cr and FY28E EBITDA is ₹420 Cr, nearer Vision-2027's ₹450 Cr.
22x is near the five-year median (22.7x), not the March 2025 peak of 41.7x.
web_blocks.takeaway: Each scenario ties a business outcome to a multiple already seen in the stock's own history. The bear and bull cases are not extremes of the band. They sit at its 25th percentile and its five-year median. That keeps the exercise honest about how far the multiple can move without a new regime.

web_blocks.caption: EPS bridge by scenario and year (₹ Cr unless stated; 1.7106 Cr shares; tax 25%; rounding to one decimal)
rows: LTM EPS at value date (average of the two years, ₹)
web_blocks.takeaway: Even the bear case has LTM EPS 15.0% above FY26's ₹101.26, because H1 FY27 EBITDA of ₹154 Cr is already banked. The bear case is a valuation story, not an earnings collapse. It needs FY27 to land on ₹300 Cr and FY28 EBITDA to fall 6% from the base FY27E. EBITDA last fell in FY20, to ₹79 Cr from ₹94 Cr.

web_blocks.the_number: Base-case LTM EPS (basis B) at the value date, about November 2027, is ₹133.9. It is the average of FY27E EPS of ₹124.5 and FY28E EPS of ₹143.4. At 18x that gives ₹2,410 per share.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Compute EPS for each year. FY27E EBITDA of ₹315 Cr less D&A of ₹36 Cr, plus other income of ₹8 Cr, less interest of ₹3 Cr gives ₹284 Cr before tax. Tax at 25% leaves ₹213.0 Cr, or ₹124.5 per share. FY28E EBITDA of ₹360 Cr less D&A of ₹38 Cr, plus ₹8 Cr, less ₹3 Cr gives ₹327 Cr before tax and ₹245.3 Cr after tax, or ₹143.4 per share. Average the two years. Shares are 1.7106 Cr.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Base FY27 EBITDA is ₹315 Cr, above the guided floor of at least ₹310 Cr. Base FY28 EBITDA is ₹360 Cr, about 14% higher. Bear uses ₹300 Cr and ₹295 Cr. Bull uses ₹330 Cr and ₹420 Cr. Tax is 25%, because the H1 FY27 rate reverted from about 20% to 25%. The share count is unchanged. Management says the ADI BPO merger cancels and reissues the same number of shares.
web_blocks.the_range: Bear LTM EPS is ₹116.4 (FY27E ₹117.9, FY28E ₹114.9). Bull LTM EPS is ₹150.4 (FY27E ₹131.1, FY28E ₹169.7). If both years' EBITDA moved by ₹10 Cr, LTM EPS would move about ₹4.4. At 18x that is about ₹79 per share, or 3.4% of today's price. Each turn of the multiple on base LTM EPS is about ₹134 per share, or 5.8% of today's price.
web_blocks.if_off: The multiple matters more than EBITDA here. A one-turn miss costs about as much as a ₹17 Cr miss in both years' EBITDA. The ₹2,150 tranche clears our 1.5-to-1 hurdle only while the base value stays at or above ₹2,367.50. On basis B the cushion is just 1.8%, equal to FY28E EBITDA of about ₹350 Cr. On basis A, the base value of ₹2,241 misses the line by ₹126.5. If Research margin holds near 48% and acquisitions close, the bull case applies. If H2 FY27 EBITDA lands below ₹156 Cr, the floor is at risk and we move weight to the bear case.

web_blocks.region_era: Netherlands, global; the AI-disruption de-rating of February to November 2026
web_blocks.mechanism: A quality, cash-generative information franchise with 83% recurring revenue was sold off on a technology-disruption narrative [65]. On 3 February 2026 Anthropic released a legal plug-in for Claude. Thomson Reuters, RELX and Wolters Kluwer fell 16%, 14% and 13% in a day. Morningstar noted that the stocks had been de-rating since summer 2025. It kept its wide-moat view that day. On 5 March 2026 it downgraded Wolters Kluwer and Thomson Reuters to a narrow moat [85]. The reported fundamentals did not move.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: FY25 revenue was €6,125m, up 6% organically. Adjusted operating margin was 27.5% (27.1% in 2024). Diluted adjusted EPS was €5.29, up 9% in constant currencies. Adjusted free cash flow was €1,348m [65]. In the first nine months of 2026, organic growth was 6% and adjusted operating profit rose 10% in constant currency. Guidance was reaffirmed on 4 November 2026 [89]. The company's own buyback prices show the multiple. The average was €128.45 in 2025 (8.6m shares, €1.1bn). It was €75.79 from January to 24 February 2026. It was €67.97 to 3 November 2026 (3.9m shares, €264m) [65, 89]. On FY25 EPS of €5.29 that is about 24.3x, 14.3x and 12.8x (desk arithmetic). The average price fell about 47% while EPS rose. Average buyback prices are a proxy for the trading price, not a quote.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: A good franchise de-rated 47% while its earnings kept rising. Either the market is right that the terminal value is impaired, or it is paying you to wait. Wolters Kluwer shows that the answer comes from organic growth and margin over the next several reporting periods, not from the multiple. MPS followed the same arc, with 41.7x falling to 16.0x while EPS rose. The twin also cuts the other way. Morningstar's narrow-moat downgrade means the de-rating was not irrational. Management puts MPS's recurring revenue at about 45% [25] against Wolters Kluwer's 83%. The case for a permanent discount is therefore stronger here.

web_blocks.html: Valuation trigger. We raise fair value only if three business metrics hold. Then the base multiple moves from 18x towards 20x, or FY28E EBITDA rises above ₹360 Cr. The first metric is H2 FY27 EBITDA of at least ₹156 Cr (the ₹310 Cr floor less H1's ₹154 Cr). The second is a Research Solutions margin of at least 45% for two further quarters. The third is a largest customer at or below 17.3% of revenue. An acquisition near 2x revenue, funded from the ₹163 Cr of cash, would also lift the bull weighting if it returns more than 25% within 12 months. We cut fair value toward the bear case on any of five events. Research margin falls below 42% for two quarters. FY27 EBITDA guidance is cut below ₹300 Cr. Corporate Learning margin slips below 18% for two quarters. A goodwill impairment above ₹25 Cr is booked. The ADI BPO scheme terms change to be dilutive to public holders.

Now to the bridge to Chapter 8. On every valuation measure above, the price is not demanding. The reverse DCF needs only about 7% to 10% a year of free-cash-flow growth over ten years. The stock trades at the five-year median multiple. The probability-weighted value is ₹2,440 on basis B and ₹2,254 on the stricter basis A. So why does the tape say wait? Because valuation does not by itself justify buying. Asymmetry is the test. The invalidation is a daily close below ₹2,005. At the ledger close of ₹2,297.00 the base-value ratio is (2,410 − 2,297) ÷ (2,297 − 2,005), or 0.39 to 1 on basis B. On basis A it is −0.19 to 1, because the base value of ₹2,241 sits below the price. The 13 Nov print of ₹2,259.30 gives 0.59 to 1 and −0.07 to 1. All of these fail our 1.5-to-1 hurdle. At the top of the support zone, ₹2,150, the ratio is 1.79 to 1 on basis B but only 0.63 to 1 on basis A. At ₹2,070 it is 5.23 to 1 on basis B and 2.63 to 1 on basis A. So the ₹2,070 level clears 1.5 to 1 on both bases, while ₹2,150 clears it only on the LTM basis. The weighted return from ₹2,150 is +13.5% on basis B and +4.8% on basis A. From ₹2,070 it is +17.9% and +8.9%. The business passes, and the price is fair. The entry point is what is missing. Chapter 8 explains why the tape offers it only lower. That tape is a Stage 3 reading in the ledger and Stage 4 in the 13 Nov snapshot. It shows a falling 50-day average and nine distribution days in 25 sessions.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with an admission that surprises people. After six chapters in which I praised this business, the valuation does not shout bargain. I wanted you to meet the company before you met the price, because a price is a mood and a business is a fact. Now we put the two side by side, and I want you to resist both of the lazy answers, the one that says great company, buy it, and the one that says it ran up, avoid it.

At the ledger close of ₹2,297 the market values all of MPS at about ₹3,929 crore. Take off the ₹163 crore of cash, add the small lease liabilities, and the business as a going concern costs about ₹3,784 crore. Against the 12 months of earnings it has actually reported, that is about 21 times profit. Against what we expect it to earn in this financial year, about 18 times. Against EBITDA, 12 to 14 times. Those are the numbers of a good business at a fair price. The company has no bank debt, converts profit into cash at about one-for-one over a decade, and earns a 35 to 39% return on capital. If you had to guess the multiple of a company like that without looking, you might say 25 or 30. You would not be far off the history, which is the point of the next few paragraphs.

Here is how I read the multiple's history. Over the last ten years the stock has traded between 4.7 and 41.7 times trailing earnings, with a median of 17.6. Over the last five years the median is 22.7. Today it is 22.7. So we sit exactly in the middle of the recent band and above the long-run median. The market is not discounting a disaster, and it is not offering a gift.

What interests me more is the journey. In March 2025 the stock was at 41.7 times trailing earnings. Twelve months later, in March 2026, it was at 16.0 times, and the price had fallen by about half, even though earnings per share had risen by a quarter. That is a lesson in what moves this stock. It is not earnings, which have risen almost every year since FY22. It is what the market thinks those earnings are worth after the next few years. And in February and March 2026 the market thought something about AI that it applied to almost everything that sells labour or content: Indian IT lost around 28% from its high, the biggest January-to-March fall since 2008, and the information publishers Thomson Reuters, RELX and Wolters Kluwer lost 13 to 16% in a single day.

I want you to hold two thoughts together. MPS's low of the year came in the same week as the sector's, so its de-rating was a sector event rather than a company event. But the peers have not recovered: Datamatics is down 18% in a year, NIIT Learning Systems down almost 50%, Newgen down almost 56%. MPS is flat. Flat sounds calm, but it hides a fall of 52% followed by a rise of 110%. When a stock does that in a year, you should not treat today's price as the anchor of a stable consensus. It is a station on a very bumpy ride.

Now the question every investor should ask before any forecast: what is this price already assuming? I call that a reverse DCF. Take the current enterprise value, decide what return you want, and work backwards to the growth rate that makes the arithmetic balance. With a 13% required return and 5% terminal growth, the market is paying for free cash flow of about ₹214 crore this year growing at roughly 12.6% in the first year and fading to 5%, about 8.8% a year on average, reaching about ₹496 crore by year ten. Does that sound heroic? To me it does not. The company grew EBITDA at 17.1% a year over the last five years and 10.2% a year over eleven. The price assumes a decade at about the lower of those two.

But please see the grid for what it is. At a 12% hurdle the answer drops to 9% in year one, and at 14% it climbs to 16%. The price is not a single number but a conversation about your required return. The discount rate matters more than any growth assumption you or I will make about the next ten years.

Set that beside what management has promised. For this financial year the CFO has raised the floor for EBITDA to at least ₹310 crore, and the first half has already delivered ₹154 crore. That alone is a rise of about 31% on last year's ₹236 crore, and my free-cash-flow starting point already includes it. Beyond this year, the company's Vision 2027 points to ₹450 crore of EBITDA in FY28, but the CEO himself says that figure combines organic growth with acquisitions. The price does not pay for it. At our base case of ₹360 crore the stock sits at only 16 times FY28 earnings, so a deal that actually lands is upside the market has not capitalised, and a deal that never comes costs the stock very little.

Now, where is the market's scepticism? It sits in four places, and I think they are the right four. First, AI price give-back: the CEO told the Q2 FY27 call, in his words, “Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume.” A 20% price cut needs 25% more volume just to stand still. Second, Research margin: it has gone from the low 40s to 48%, and on last year's revenue each point is worth about ₹4.6 crore, so a return to 40% would cost roughly ₹37 crore of EBITDA. Third, concentration: one customer is more than a sixth of revenue. Fourth, acquisition accounting: more than half the balance sheet is goodwill and intangibles. None of that is an accounting flaw. All of it is a reason why this stock has not been, and should not be, paid 41 times again.

That brings us to the scenarios. We value the stock twelve months out, in about November 2027. A trailing multiple must be applied to trailing earnings, so I show you two readings. The first, which I call basis A, uses the last full fiscal year's EPS, which is how the band itself was built. At that date it is FY27's EPS. The second, basis B, uses the last twelve months of earnings, the average of the FY27 and FY28 estimates. Basis B is my central case because markets price on current earnings. Basis A is the stress case. On basis B, the bear case has EBITDA of ₹300 crore this year and ₹295 crore next. Trailing EPS is ₹116.4, and a 14 times multiple (near the 25th percentile of the band) gives about ₹1,630, 29% below today. The base case has EBITDA of ₹315 crore and then ₹360 crore. Trailing EPS is ₹133.9, and 18 times (near the median) gives about ₹2,410, 5% above today. The bull case has ₹330 crore and then ₹420 crore. Trailing EPS is ₹150.4, and 22 times (near the five-year median) gives about ₹3,310, 44% above. Weight them 25, 50 and 25 and you get ₹2,440, 6% above the close. On basis A the same weights give ₹2,254, 2% below the close, and the base value is ₹2,241.

Be honest about what these numbers mean. A 6% expected return from today's price on the generous basis, and a small loss on the strict one, is thin for a business of this quality. The base case gives 5% on basis B and minus 2% on basis A. The bear case gives minus 29% or minus 28%. A margin of safety is not an expected return; it is how much you can be wrong and still be fine, and at ₹2,297 you cannot be very wrong. Enter lower and the weighted returns are 13.5% from ₹2,150 and nearly 18% from ₹2,070 on basis B, and 4.8% and 8.9% on basis A. The weights are a judgment too. Move to 35, 45 and 20 and the basis B value drops to about ₹2,317. The decision does not hang on the weights. It hangs on reward-to-risk at the support zone.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: a multiple is a mood about the years after next
book_callouts.quote: When earnings rise by a quarter and the multiple falls by sixty percent, the market is not disagreeing about next year; it is changing its mind about the years after that.
book_callouts.text: The 2026 AI debate was a debate about terminal value. Nobody can forecast whether production vendors will keep a margin in 2032, so the multiple swung from 41.7 times to 16.0 times and back to 28.9 times inside eighteen months. The right response is neither to buy the fear nor to wait for certainty. It is to ask what the price assumes about the years after next and whether our evidence is better or worse than that assumption.
bullets: The price already assumes about 7 to 10% annual free-cash-flow growth for a decade, which is below recent delivery.
The discount rate you choose decides the answer more than any growth forecast.
The multiple, not earnings, is the volatile variable in this stock.

book_subsections.title: The Twin: Wolters Kluwer's Year of Falling Multiples
paragraphs: Every investor wants to know whether a drama has happened before. The best case I can show you comes from this very year. Wolters Kluwer is a Dutch information company with 83% of revenue recurring. It sells tax, legal, health and compliance software and content to professionals. In 2025 its revenue was €6.1 billion, up 6% organically; its adjusted operating margin was 27.5%; its adjusted earnings per share were €5.29, up 9% in constant currencies.

Then came 3 February 2026. Anthropic released a legal plug-in for its Claude assistant, and in a single day Thomson Reuters fell 16%, RELX 14% and Wolters Kluwer 13%. Morningstar's analyst wrote that the stocks had already de-rated sharply over the previous year and that the plug-in had nothing to do with legal research, the heart of those businesses. A month later, the same house cut its moat rating on two of the three to narrow. Which of the two views is right? That is precisely the argument.

Here is what the company's own buyback prices say. In 2025 Wolters Kluwer bought back 8.6 million shares at an average €128.45. In the first weeks of 2026 the average was €75.79, and by 3 November 2026 the year-to-date average was €67.97. Divide by the 2025 earnings of €5.29 and the multiple went from about 24 times to about 14 times and then about 13 times. A drop of roughly 47% in the average price, while earnings kept growing and the nine-month update on 4 November reported organic growth of 6% and adjusted operating profit up 10%.

Does it map to MPS? Partly. MPS also saw its multiple fall by 60% while earnings rose. But I want you to notice the difference. Wolters Kluwer's revenue is mostly recurring software and content with high switching costs. MPS has a large book of production work whose unit price AI is pushing down, plus platforms and a medical-knowledge asset that look more like Wolters Kluwer. The market's decision to charge MPS a lower multiple than it used to is not irrational. The question is whether it charges too low a multiple, and the way to answer is the same one Wolters Kluwer's investors face: wait for the next several reporting periods and watch organic growth and margin.

book_subsections.title: Peers: Why 'Cheap' Is the Wrong Word
paragraphs: Let me walk you through the three Indian peers, because the table says something subtler than the word cheap. Datamatics has a 15.9% operating margin and a 20% return on capital. NIIT Learning Systems has a 12.9% margin and a return of about 21%. Newgen has a 23.7% margin and 25%. MPS has a 29.5% margin and 38.7% return on capital with almost no debt. MPS is the best business of the four by every measure, and the market pays a P/E of about 20.7, barely above Datamatics at 18.9.

You might reasonably say: so MPS must be cheap against its peers. I would say: look at what the peers have done in a year. They are down 18, 50 and 56%. The market has been taking a hammer to this whole group, and the peers are not recovering. MPS's flat one-year move already includes a spectacular rebound. The peers are cheaper because their multiples are still being compressed; MPS's has partly bounced back.

The global names teach the rest. RWS, the language-services company, lost about six points of margin in a single year as machine translation cut unit prices, and had to write off £88 million of goodwill. That is what deflation looks like when it arrives. Skillsoft's revenue fell 6% in a quarter, a reminder of what corporate learning can do. Innodata grew 53% in the latest quarter at an 18.5% EBITDA margin, which shows AI creating demand for human judgment but with project contracts that can be cancelled at will. And Wolters Kluwer Health earns a 32% margin by selling expert-written clinical content that now sits inside an AI product. MPS's FY26 margin of 30.7% lies in the middle of that range, and the whole question is which side of it the company ends up on.

book_subsections.title: From Fair Price to the Wait: The Bridge to the Tape
paragraphs: Let me end by tying this chapter to the next, because the two together produce the decision. On valuation, the price is not demanding. The reverse DCF needs a decade of free-cash-flow growth that the company has comfortably beaten over five years, the multiple sits at its five-year median and the probability-weighted value is ₹2,440. If valuation alone were the test, it would argue for owning the stock.

But asymmetry is the test that matters, and it is mathematical. Our invalidation is a daily close below ₹2,005, under the 200-day average. The base value is ₹2,410 on basis B and ₹2,241 on basis A. At ₹2,297 you would risk ₹292 per share to make ₹113 on basis B. That is a ratio of 0.39 to 1. On basis A the base value is below the price, so the ratio is minus 0.19 to 1. Both fail our 1.5 hurdle. At the 13 November print of ₹2,259.30 the ratios are 0.59 and minus 0.07, still short. At the top of our support zone, ₹2,150, you would risk ₹145 to make ₹260 on basis B, a ratio of 1.79 to 1. On basis A you would make only ₹91, a ratio of 0.63 to 1. At ₹2,070 you would risk ₹65 to make ₹340 on basis B and ₹171 on basis A. The ratios are 5.23 and 2.63. So ₹2,070 clears the hurdle on both bases, and ₹2,150 clears it only on basis B. Same business, same targets, different entry price. Note how thin the ₹2,150 cushion is. That tranche needs a base value of at least ₹2,367.50. Basis B clears it by 1.8% and basis A misses it by ₹126.5.

This is why I say the business passes and the price does not yet. A fair price is not a reason to buy, because fair prices are common. A fair price with a reward at least one and a half times the risk is rarer, and the tape in Chapter 8 will show you why it may well be offered lower. The CEO said on the Q2 FY27 call that “I would rather miss a deal than overpay.” (Chairman and CEO Rahul Arora, Q2 FY27) It is the right instinct for a company buying companies, and it is a good rule for those of us buying the company.
